teach.title: What it does

notice.ask: Tap the verb in each sentence that says what had already happened. What do the two endings have in common?

teach.say: For something already over before the past thing you are telling about, Latin has **the pluperfect subjunctive (the 'had / would have' form: cum vēnisset = when he had come)**. It follows *cum*, a question word, *sī* or *utinam*, never standing alone as a plain statement. In pfs-01 the dining is finished before the sleeping begins, and *cēnāvissent* says so.

check.ask: Tap the verb that names what had already happened before Aemilia was glad.

teach.title: Building the singular: -issem, -issēs, -isset
teach.say: Take the perfect infinitive (the 'to have done' form) — *scrīpsisse* — and hang the personal endings on it: *scrīpsisse-m*, *scrīpsissē-s*, *scrīpsisse-t*. The third person singular ends in **-isset**, and that is the form you meet most, so that is the cell opened here. Every verb does it this way, however odd its perfect: *fuisset*, *potuisset*, *voluisset*.

check.ask: Write the pluperfect subjunctive, third person singular.

teach.title: The plural: -issēmus, -issētis, -issent
teach.say: The plural adds the person endings you already know: **-issēmus** (we), **-issētis** (you all), **-issent** (they). Nothing new but those endings — the *-isse-* in the middle never moves and never changes. The cell opened here is 'you all', **-issētis**.

check.ask: Write the pluperfect subjunctive, second person plural.

teach.title: The passive is two words
teach.say: In the passive the form splits: the perfect participle (a verb used like an adjective — *scrīptus*, written) plus *essem, essēs, esset*. The participle agrees with its subject, so its ending follows the noun: *epistula scrīpta esset*, but *Mārcus laudātus esset*.

check.ask: scrīpta esset — which tense, mood and voice is it?

teach.title: Telling it from the imperfect subjunctive
teach.say: Both follow a past main verb and are easily swapped. The imperfect subjunctive (the past-time 'might / would' form: *venīret*) is built on the plain infinitive and means 'while it was going on'; the pluperfect is built on the perfect infinitive and means 'after it was over'. The test is quick: look for **-isse-** inside the word.

check.ask: audīvisset — which tense is it, and which letters in the middle told you?

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: After *cum* it puts a story in order: first this had happened, then that. *Cum* can also mean 'since' — the same subjunctive, giving the reason instead of the order of events: *cum Mārcus laudātus esset, laetus erat*. After *sī* it makes an unreal past — *sī tacuissēs, magister tē laudāvisset*, and neither half happened. After *utinam* it is a regret.

core.text: For an action already finished before a past main verb, the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do) becomes **the pluperfect subjunctive (the 'had / would have' form: cum venisset = when he had come)**. Build it from the perfect infinitive (the 'to have done' form), *vēnisse*, plus the personal endings: *vēnisse-m, vēnissē-s, vēnisse-t, vēnissē-mus, vēnissē-tis, vēnisse-nt*; passive: perfect participle + *essem, essēs, esset* (*captus esset*). Latin name: *coniūnctīvus plūsquamperfectī*.
English 'had done' in a story: *when he had said this, he left*; and 'would have' in unreal pasts: *if he had drunk, he would not have died*.
Perfect infinitive + endings (-issem … -issent). After a past main verb, for what had already happened: cum clauses, indirect questions, past wishes, unreal past conditions.

invented.en: When they had dined, they went to bed.
I did not know who had come.

core.text: Both follow a past main verb. The imperfect subjunctive (the past-time 'might / would' form: veniret; built on the infinitive) is for something going on at the same time — 'while he was coming'; the pluperfect, built on the perfect infinitive (*vēnisset*), is for something already over — 'after he had come'. Look for -isse- inside the word.

more.text: Also easy to confuse: *vēnisse* on its own is the perfect infinitive, used in reported statements — *dīcit eum vēnisse*, he says that he came. Add -m, -s, -t and it becomes the pluperfect subjunctive. Same stem, different job: infinitive after 'says / thinks', subjunctive after cum / sī / utinam / a question word.

The learner's notes: just as the perfect subjunctive stands in for the present, the pluperfect stands in for the imperfect to add a sense of completion; 2nd stem + *-isse-* + *-m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt* (*cēpissem*), looking exactly like the perfect infinitive with endings; passive 3rd stem + *essem, essēs, esset* (*captus essem*). Uses: causal (*nōn poteram exīre cum aliquis portam clausisset* — I could not go out since someone had shut the gate), indirect question (*nesciēbam quis advēnisset*), and narrative (*hōc cum dīxisset, profectus est* — after he had said this, he left; *cum multitūdinem piscium cēpissent, ad lītus rediērunt*).

Ørberg's chapter 33: *Iūlius dubitābat num magister Mārcum laudāvisset*, and the unreal past *sī bonus discipulus fuissēs, magister tē laudāvisset* — if you had been a good pupil, the teacher would have praised you. Irregulars: *fuissem, potuissem, voluissem, īssem*. The passive uses *essem*, the imperfect subjunctive of *sum*: *laudātus essem* is 'I had been praised / I would have been praised', never 'I was being praised'.
